scenes.name: hook
scenes.text: A metro train glides in, and stops with its doors lined up almost exactly with the platform gates. How?

scenes.name: where
scenes.text: The train counts wheel turns to track distance. But wheels can slip, so beacons on the track, called balises, correct its position.

scenes.name: talk
scenes.text: On many new lines, a system called CBTC lets each train constantly radio its position and speed to a control centre.

scenes.name: gap
scenes.text: The control system works out how far ahead each train can safely go, and sends it a limit. That keeps trains apart.

scenes.name: atp
scenes.text: If a train goes faster than its limit allows, automatic train protection applies the brakes on its own.

scenes.name: ato
scenes.text: Automatic train operation brakes along a smooth curve, using beacons near the platform, to stop right on the mark.

scenes.name: doors
scenes.text: Only once it has stopped in the right spot, do the train doors and the platform gates open together.

scenes.name: outro
scenes.text: Wheels, beacons, radio, brakes. Stopping on the dot. Follow for more on how things really work.
